name: Pes anserine tendinopathy / bursitis
aka: medial knee pain below the joint line
populations: middle-aged and older women, often with knee osteoarthritis
people with obesity or type 2 diabetes (association inconsistent)
runners and athletes who repeat knee flexion
adolescents with a medial proximal tibial osteochondroma (rare)
summary: Pain over the medial proximal tibia where sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus insert. The bursitis label is contested: imaging rarely shows bursal fluid, and osteoarthritis and meniscal pain overlap.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Not established. Trials followed patients for only 1–8 weeks after injection or shockwave, and no trial of exercise or stretching was found

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: No validated criteria. Return is guided by pain, tolerance of loading and exclusion of other medial knee pathology (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Focal tenderness over the pes anserine insertion. Compared with MRI, clinical diagnosis had sensitivity 41.2% and specificity 59.5% in 156 patients

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI showed pes anserine bursitis in only 2.5% of 509 symptomatic knees; ultrasound showed it in 20% of knees in a symptomatic osteoarthritis cohort

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Mostly middle-aged to older women in the published series. All 22 cases in one case-control study were women with a mean age of 62

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Anserine bursa tenderness was reported by 33.3% of 3,654 people with or at risk of knee osteoarthritis. True bursitis is far less common

overview:
Pes anserine pain is pain over the anteromedial proximal tibia, where the conjoined tendons of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus insert [r1]. It is usually called pes anserine tendinitis or bursitis, but that label is contested. On MRI, pes anserine bursitis was found in only 2.5% of 509 symptomatic knees, and the commonest clinical presentation was medial joint-line pain mimicking a medial meniscal tear [r2]. On ultrasound, only 2 patients (8.7%) with a clinical diagnosis and knee osteoarthritis showed bursitis or tendinitis [r3], and in 37 suspected cases tendinitis was seen in one symptomatic knee and bursitis in two [r4]. A recent review concludes that structural bursitis is confirmed in only a minority of cases, so management relies on clinical assessment [r5].

The diagnosis is also unreliable. Against MRI findings, a clinical diagnosis of pes anserine tendinitis-bursitis syndrome had sensitivity 41.2% and specificity 59.5% in 156 patients, and clinically diagnosed patients did not differ in MRI bursitis, meniscal or ligament lesions from those without the diagnosis; their medial joint space was narrower [r6]. The condition overlaps with knee osteoarthritis: ultrasound bursitis was found in 20% of knees in symptomatic osteoarthritis and rose with radiographic grade [r7]. Treat the label as a working description of medial tibial pain, and exclude medial compartment disease first.

Treatment evidence is limited. Three small randomised trials (60 to 180 patients) compared corticosteroid injection with shockwave, platelet-rich plasma, ozone or dextrose, with follow-up of 8 weeks or less and no placebo arm [r8,r9,r10]. No trial of exercise, stretching or manual therapy was identified, so physiotherapy rests on expert opinion and on the review's description of standard care [r5].

epidemiology.text: True incidence is unknown because the diagnosis is clinical and imaging rarely confirms it. In a retrospective MRI review of 509 knee studies from 488 patients with knee pain, pes anserine bursitis was reported in 2.5% [r2]. In the Osteoarthritis Initiative, 33.3% of 3,654 participants with or at risk of knee osteoarthritis had tenderness or pain over the anserine bursa, and this was associated with incident falls over 2 years (OR 1.188, 95% CI 1.021–1.383) [r11]. In 85 patients with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis (170 knees), ultrasound bursitis was present in 20% of knees, was more frequent in women and older patients, and correlated with radiographic grade [r7]. In 37 patients with suspected pes anserine tendino-bursitis, all were women, 93% had radiographic osteoarthritis and 75% had a BMI over 27 [r4]. In a case-control study of 22 clinically diagnosed women (mean age 62.1), diabetes, osteoarthritis and obesity did not differ from controls, whereas valgus knee deformity did (OR 5.2, 95% CI 1.1–25.5) [r12]. A review lists osteoarthritis, obesity, type 2 diabetes and athletes who repeat knee flexion as high-risk groups [r5].

intrinsic: Female sex and older age: all cases in two small series were women [r4,r12], and ultrasound bursitis was more frequent in women and older patients in osteoarthritis [r7]
Knee osteoarthritis: bursa size correlated with radiographic grade [r7], but osteoarthritis prevalence did not differ between 22 cases and 38 controls [r12], so the link is inconsistent
Valgus knee deformity (OR 5.2), alone or with collateral instability (OR 6.0) in a small case-control study [r12]
Obesity and type 2 diabetes: listed as high-risk groups in a review [r5], although neither differed from controls in a case-control study [r12]
A medial proximal tibial osteochondroma, which can cause pes anserine syndrome in adolescents [r13]
extrinsic: Repetitive knee flexion, as in athletes who run or cycle [r5]
Sudden rises in running or cycling load (clinical reasoning; modifiable, but no study of load spikes in this condition was found)
Tight or overloaded hamstring, gracilis and sartorius muscles are often proposed as contributors (clinical teaching; no sourced test of this)

mechanism.summary: Pes anserine pain has no single injury moment. The usual proposal is overuse: repeated knee flexion and valgus loading make the conjoined tendons pull and glide over the medial proximal tibia, irritating the tendon insertion or the bursa beneath it [r5]. Valgus knee deformity was associated with the diagnosis (OR 5.2) in a small case-control study [r12]. This mechanism is a clinical model: the tissue source of pain has not been shown, and no biomechanical study was identified.
sequence: The person increases repetitive knee flexion, such as running, cycling, stairs or prolonged walking, often with a valgus knee position [r5,r12].
At each flexion cycle the sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus tendons pull and glide over the medial proximal tibia and the structures beneath them [r1].
Repeated load or friction irritates the tendon insertion, the bursa between the tendons and the tibia, or both (proposed, not proven) [r5].
The area becomes tender, and pain appears with stairs, getting up from a chair and prolonged flexion.
Ultrasound or MRI may show tendon change or fluid beneath the tendons, but in most people with typical symptoms they show neither [r2,r3].
Overlapping medial compartment osteoarthritis, a meniscal tear or collateral ligament pain can produce a similar picture, which makes the true source hard to establish [r2,r6].

variants.name: Athletic overuse
variants.description: Athletes who repeat knee flexion are a recognised group, and management focuses on load and biomechanics [r5].

variants.name: Osteoarthritis-associated pain
variants.description: Anserine bursa tenderness is common in knee osteoarthritis (33.3% in the Osteoarthritis Initiative), and ultrasound bursitis (20% of knees) rose with radiographic grade [r11,r7].

variants.name: Mechanical irritation from a tibial osteochondroma
variants.description: A medial proximal tibial exostosis can irritate the tendons and bursa. In 21 adolescents with this lesion, surgical excision improved IKDC scores [r13].

variants.name: Snapping pes anserine syndrome
variants.description: A reported case had posteromedial snapping, a normal MRI apart from mild bursal fluid, no response to 6 weeks of physiotherapy and dynamic ultrasound showing the tendons sliding across a mass [r14].

variants.name: After knee arthroplasty
variants.description: Pes anserine syndrome has been reported after total knee arthroplasty, treated with stretching and steroid injection in a single case report [r15].

anatomy.text: The pes anserinus is the conjoined insertion of the sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus tendons on the anteromedial proximal tibia, and it is often neglected during imaging assessment [r1]. In a cadaveric study of 86 legs, the sartorius inserted into a superficial layer, whereas the gracilis and semitendinosus inserted into a deeper layer. The semitendinosus had one tendon at the insertion in 66% of specimens, two in 31% and three in 3%. The anserine bursa was irregularly circular and lay posterior and superior to the tibial midline, following the line of the sartorius [r16]. The bursa sits between the conjoined tendons and the proximal tibia [r5]. The medial collateral ligament and the medial joint line lie close by, which helps explain how the pain mimics medial knee pathology.

structures.name: Sartorius tendon
structures.role: Superficial layer of the pes anserinus. The muscle flexes and externally rotates the hip and flexes the knee [r16]

structures.name: Gracilis tendon
structures.role: Deeper layer of the insertion. Adducts the hip and flexes and medially rotates the knee [r16]

structures.name: Semitendinosus tendon
structures.role: Deeper layer, with one to three tendon slips at the insertion. Extends the hip, flexes the knee and rotates it medially [r16]

structures.name: Anserine bursa
structures.role: A bursa between the conjoined tendons and the proximal tibia. It is usually not visible on ultrasound or MRI unless it contains fluid [r5,r2]

structures.name: Medial proximal tibia
structures.role: The insertion site, where tenderness is felt. A medial tibial osteochondroma can irritate the area [r13]

structures.name: Medial collateral ligament and medial joint line
structures.role: Neighbouring structures that can cause overlapping medial knee pain and must be distinguished [r2]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
The tissue source of pes anserine pain has not been established. Three explanations compete: tendinopathy or enthesopathy of the conjoined tendons from overload, inflammation of the bursa beneath them, and referred or overlapping pain from medial compartment disease. Imaging argues against bursitis as the usual source. MRI found bursitis in 2.5% of 509 symptomatic knees [r2]. Ultrasound showed bursitis or tendinitis in only 2 clinically diagnosed osteoarthritis patients (8.7%) [r3], and in 37 suspected cases tendinitis occurred in one symptomatic knee and bursitis in two symptomatic knees and one asymptomatic knee [r4]. When bursitis is present on MRI, it appears as fluid beneath the tendons at the medial tibia near the joint line [r17]. In 156 patients, clinically diagnosed and undiagnosed patients did not differ in MRI bursitis, effusion, meniscal or ligament lesions, although the medial joint space was narrower in the diagnosed group [r6].

The relationship to treatment response is also unclear. After corticosteroid injection in 17 osteoarthritis patients with a clinical diagnosis, pain and WOMAC scores improved significantly, but the two patients with the best response were the two with ultrasound bursitis; most improved patients had no ultrasound abnormality [r3]. Pain from the area is therefore best treated as medial tibial pain with an unproven source. Anserine bursa tenderness is also common in knee osteoarthritis and was linked to a higher risk of falls [r11,r7].

structures.name: Pes anserine tendons (insertion)
structures.effect: Proposed tendinopathy or enthesopathy from overload. Tendinitis was seen on ultrasound in only one symptomatic knee in a series of 37 [r4]. No histology was identified.

structures.name: Anserine bursa
structures.effect: Fluid beneath the tendons near the medial joint line when bursitis is present [r17], but this was found on MRI in only 2.5% of symptomatic knees [r2]

structures.name: Medial compartment (joint space, meniscus, cartilage)
structures.effect: Narrower medial joint space in clinically diagnosed patients [r6]. Pain frequently mimics a medial meniscal tear [r2]

structures.name: Proximal tibia
structures.effect: A medial tibial osteochondroma can cause the same syndrome in adolescents [r13]

muscles.name: Semitendinosus, gracilis and sartorius
muscles.effect: Tightness or overload is often proposed. No study in the sources reviewed tested hamstring or gracilis flexibility against outcome (clinical teaching).

muscles.name: Quadriceps and hip abductors
muscles.effect: Pain inhibition and reduced control of the knee in valgus are plausible. Valgus deformity was associated with the diagnosis (OR 5.2) [r12].

muscles.name: Calf and foot muscles
muscles.effect: Foot posture and ankle mechanics change the load on the medial knee (clinical reasoning; no sourced test).

cellular.timing: Days to weeks of repetitive loading
cellular.description: Repeated tendon glide and tension over the medial tibia irritates the tendon insertion and bursa. This is a model, not confirmed by biopsy [r5].
Local swelling and tenderness. Synovial inflammation of the bursa has not been shown in most patients with typical symptoms [r2,r3].
Fluid beneath the tendons can occur in a minority and is visible on MRI or ultrasound [r17,r7].
Natural history studies were not identified. Most patients are treated conservatively [r5].

systems.effect: Local tenderness over the tibia can be sensitised, and nearby nerve irritation (infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve) is a differential (clinical teaching). No pain-processing study was identified.
Valgus knee deformity, alone or with collateral instability, was associated with the diagnosis (OR 5.2 and 6.0) in a small case-control study [r12].
Obesity and type 2 diabetes are listed as high-risk groups in a review [r5], but did not differ from controls in a case-control study [r12].
Knee osteoarthritis overlaps: bursa size correlated with radiographic grade [r7], and medial joint space was narrower in clinically diagnosed patients [r6].
Anserine bursa pain was associated with incident falls over 2 years in osteoarthritis (OR 1.188) [r11].

timeframes.summary: Natural history and recovery times are not established. No longitudinal study was identified, and the randomised trials followed patients for only 1 to 8 weeks [r8,r9]. A review describes response to injection as commonly assessed at 8 weeks [r5]. The phases below are clinical convention and not from outcome data.

healing.description: Pain with stairs and provocative loading; reduce the aggravating load and settle symptoms (clinical convention)
Pain and function were measured at 1 and 8 weeks after injection or shockwave [r8,r9]
Progressive loading of the knee, hip and thigh muscles, with no trial evidence for exercise in this condition (clinical convention)
Graded return to running or cycling guided by pain and by exclusion of other medial knee pathology (clinical convention)

milestones.label: First response check
milestones.note: Trials measured pain at 1 week after injection or shockwave [r8,r9]

milestones.label: Reconsider the diagnosis if not improving
milestones.note: Clinical convention. Consider ultrasound or MRI for another source, especially in an older patient with osteoarthritis [r2,r6]

milestones.label: Response to injection commonly judged
milestones.note: A review describes 8 weeks as the usual point at which response is assessed [r5]

milestones.label: Escalate if symptoms persist
milestones.note: Clinical convention. Surgery is considered only after conservative measures are exhausted [r5]

milestones.label: Typical return to full loading
milestones.note: Clinical convention; no outcome data identified

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based and not time-based. No return-to-sport studies were identified. In practice, return to running or cycling follows a pain-guided, graded loading program once other medial knee pathology has been excluded (clinical convention).

symptoms: Pain on the anteromedial proximal tibia, just below the medial joint line, often described as medial knee pain [r1,r5]
Pain that mimics a medial meniscal tear: medial joint-line pain was the commonest presentation on MRI-confirmed bursitis [r2]
Pain with stairs, getting up from a chair, walking and repeated knee flexion, as in running or cycling (clinical teaching)
Gradual onset over weeks, often in a middle-aged or older woman with knee osteoarthritis, or in an athlete after a rise in training load [r4,r5]
Pain that may disturb sleep when the knees touch in bed (clinical teaching)
signs: Focal tenderness over the pes anserine insertion on the anteromedial proximal tibia [r5]
Little or no visible swelling in most people. A fluid collection is seen on imaging in a minority [r2,r17]
Full knee range of motion and no joint-line effusion unless an intra-articular problem coexists
Pain on resisted knee flexion or on stretching the hamstrings and sartorius (clinical teaching)
No clear collateral instability, and a negative McMurray test and valgus stress test, if the pain is isolated

subjective: Pain location (anteromedial proximal tibia below the joint line), aggravating activities and night pain [r5]
Age, sex and weight, and a history of knee osteoarthritis, diabetes or obesity [r4,r5]
Training history: recent rise in running, cycling or stair load, and repetitive knee flexion [r5]
Mechanical symptoms (locking, catching, giving way) that point to a meniscal or ligament cause [r2]
Previous injections and their effect: relief after an injection does not prove the diagnosis [r3]
Medial knee anatomy red flags: a hard, fixed mass (osteochondroma) or snapping [r13,r14]
Falls history, because anserine bursa pain was associated with incident falls in osteoarthritis [r11]
observation: Leg alignment: valgus knee deformity, foot posture and pelvic control in stance (valgus deformity was associated with the diagnosis) [r12]
Medial knee swelling or a visible mass; true swelling is uncommon [r2]
Gait and single-leg squat: dynamic valgus, trunk lean and reduced knee flexion
Quadriceps and thigh bulk compared with the other side
palpation: Focal tenderness over the pes anserine insertion, on the anteromedial proximal tibia below the joint line [r5]. Tenderness alone is not specific: clinical diagnosis against MRI had sensitivity 41.2% and specificity 59.5% [r6]
Joint-line tenderness and the medial collateral ligament, to separate meniscal and ligament sources [r2]
Medial femoral condyle, medial tibial plateau and the tibial shaft for bony tenderness or a prominence [r13]
Check along the line of the sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus tendons for tenderness and snapping [r16,r14]
rangeOfMotion: Knee flexion and extension, usually full. Loss of motion or an effusion suggests an intra-articular cause
Hamstring, gracilis and sartorius length, and hip rotation. No study tested whether flexibility predicts outcome (clinical teaching)
Ankle dorsiflexion and foot posture, which alter load on the medial knee (clinical reasoning)
strength: Resisted knee flexion with tibial internal rotation, noting reproduction of the medial tibial pain (clinical teaching)
Quadriceps, hip abductor and calf strength, and single-leg control
Isometric hamstring strength with pain rating, to guide loading
neuro: Sensation over the medial leg and the infrapatellar saphenous branch distribution, to exclude saphenous nerve irritation (clinical convention)
functional: Stair climb and descent, and sit-to-stand, with pain rating
Single-leg squat and step-down: dynamic valgus and pain
Running or cycling provocation in athletes, with pain rating
Sport-specific tasks: changes of direction and repeated knee flexion

specialTests.name: Clinical diagnosis of pes anserine tendinitis-bursitis (history plus tenderness over the insertion)
specialTests.purpose: Identify medial proximal tibial pain consistent with the syndrome
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the pes anserine insertion on the anteromedial proximal tibia with the knee relaxed, and compare with the other side. Ask whether this reproduces the familiar pain.
specialTests.positive: Focal tenderness at the insertion reproducing the pain. In 156 patients, clinical diagnosis relative to MRI findings had sensitivity 41.2% and specificity 59.5%, so a positive finding does not confirm bursitis or tendinitis.

specialTests.name: Resisted knee flexion with tibial internal rotation
specialTests.purpose: Load the pes anserine tendons and reproduce the pain
specialTests.procedure: With the person prone and the knee flexed to about 45°, ask for knee flexion with medial rotation of the tibia against resistance.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of the familiar medial tibial pain. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Valgus stress test at 0° and 30°
specialTests.purpose: Exclude a medial collateral ligament sprain, a mimic of medial knee pain
specialTests.procedure: Apply a valgus force to the knee in extension and at 30° of flexion and compare laxity and pain with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Pain at the joint line or laxity suggests the medial collateral ligament rather than the pes anserine insertion. No accuracy figures were identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Medial joint-line palpation and McMurray test
specialTests.purpose: Exclude a medial meniscal tear, the usual mimic [r2]
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the medial joint line in 90° of flexion. Perform a McMurray test if the history suggests a mechanical problem.
specialTests.positive: Joint-line tenderness or a painful click suggests a meniscal tear. Pes anserine bursitis most often presented as medial joint-line pain mimicking a medial meniscal tear on MRI [r2]. No accuracy figures were quoted here.

clinicalRules.name: No validated criteria
clinicalRules.description: A review notes the absence of a validated quantitative clinical assessment tool, and the condition remains a clinical diagnosis requiring careful history, examination and selective imaging [r5].

clinicalRules.name: Diagnosis of exclusion
clinicalRules.description: Because clinical diagnosis had sensitivity 41.2% and specificity 59.5% against MRI [r6], exclude medial meniscal, collateral ligament, medial compartment osteoarthritis, bone and nerve causes before settling on a pes anserine source [r2].

outcomeMeasures.name: Pain visual analogue or numerical rating scale
outcomeMeasures.use: Primary outcome in the injection and shockwave trials at 1 and 8 weeks [r8,r9]

outcomeMeasures.name: WOMAC pain and function
outcomeMeasures.use: Used in knee osteoarthritis cohorts and in the randomised trials [r8,r3]

outcomeMeasures.name: Ritchie articular index (tenderness)
outcomeMeasures.use: Used to grade tenderness around the knee at baseline, 1 week and 8 weeks in one randomised trial [r8]

outcomeMeasures.name: Functional tests (stair climb, sit-to-stand, single-leg squat)
outcomeMeasures.use: Clinical measures of function and dynamic valgus; track change over time (clinical convention)

imaging.indication: To grade knee osteoarthritis and to look for a tibial osteochondroma or exostosis, especially in adolescents or with a palpable mass
imaging.findings: Medial joint space narrowing in clinically diagnosed patients [r6]. A pedunculated medial proximal tibial osteochondroma can cause the syndrome [r13].

imaging.indication: To look for fluid beneath the tendons or tendon change, to guide injection, and to assess dynamic snapping [r14,r18]
imaging.findings: Bursitis was found in 20% of knees in a symptomatic osteoarthritis cohort [r7], but only 2 of the clinically diagnosed patients (8.7%) in another series [r3].

imaging.indication: When the picture is atypical, mechanical symptoms are present or other pathology is suspected
imaging.findings: Fluid beneath the pes anserinus tendons near the medial joint line, seen in 2.5% of 509 symptomatic knees [r2,r17]. Axial images help separate the bursa from other medial fluid collections [r2].

differentials.name: Medial meniscal tear
differentials.distinguishing: Mechanical symptoms (catching, locking), joint-line tenderness, a positive McMurray test and effusion. Pes anserine bursitis commonly mimics a meniscal tear on presentation [r2].

differentials.name: Degenerative medial meniscal tear or medial compartment osteoarthritis
differentials.distinguishing: Older patient with joint-space narrowing and joint-line pain. Medial joint space was narrower in clinically diagnosed pes anserine patients, so the conditions overlap [r6].

differentials.name: Medial collateral ligament sprain
differentials.distinguishing: A valgus injury, tenderness along the ligament and laxity or pain on valgus stress.

differentials.name: Patellofemoral pain
differentials.distinguishing: Anterior or peripatellar pain, worse with stairs, squatting and prolonged sitting, without focal tenderness at the tibial insertion.

differentials.name: Tibial stress fracture or bone injury of the medial plateau
differentials.distinguishing: Focal bony tenderness, pain at rest or at night and a rise in load. A radiograph or MRI shows it.

differentials.name: Medial proximal tibial osteochondroma
differentials.distinguishing: A palpable bony prominence and a pedunculated lesion on radiograph in an adolescent or young adult [r13].

differentials.name: Snapping pes anserine tendons or a ganglion cyst
differentials.distinguishing: A painful snapping sensation or a soft-tissue mass. Dynamic ultrasound showed the tendons sliding across a mass in a reported case [r14].

differentials.name: Saphenous nerve irritation
differentials.distinguishing: Burning or shooting pain and sensory change over the medial leg, rather than load-related focal tendon tenderness (clinical teaching).

redFlags: A hot, red, swollen knee or medial knee with fever or inability to bear weight: suspect septic bursitis, septic arthritis or a fracture. Refer the same day for emergency assessment.

Constant pain unrelated to load, night pain or pain at rest, especially with unexplained weight loss or a history of cancer: suspect a bone tumour, infection or stress fracture. Arrange urgent imaging and medical review.
A hard, fixed mass or a bony prominence on the medial tibia, especially in an adolescent: arrange a radiograph and orthopaedic review for osteochondroma or another tumour [r13].
Locking, giving way or a large effusion: look for a meniscal or ligament injury rather than a bursal cause [r2].
Skin infection or redness over the injection site, or an unwell patient: do not inject. Infection of skin or soft tissue is the main contraindication to injection [r18].
Calf pain, swelling or warmth in the medial leg with a recent injury or immobility: exclude deep vein thrombosis the same day.

management.principles: Treat pes anserine pain as a clinical diagnosis with an uncertain tissue source. Exclude medial compartment osteoarthritis, a meniscal tear, collateral ligament injury, bone and nerve causes first, because the clinical diagnosis was wrong more often than right against MRI [r6,r2]. The standard of care described in a recent review is rest, ice and short-term NSAIDs, then physical therapy, and an intrabursal corticosteroid injection if symptoms persist, with response judged at 8 weeks; surgery follows only after these measures fail [r5]. The evidence behind each step is weak. The three randomised trials compared active treatments with each other, without placebo and with 8 weeks or less of follow-up [r8,r9,r10]. No trial of exercise or stretching was found, so physiotherapy is guided by clinical reasoning and by addressing contributing factors such as alignment, load and weight [r5,r12]. Decide with the patient and review at about 8 weeks.

medical.name: Relative rest, ice and short-term NSAIDs
medical.description: Described as the first step of standard care in a recent review, with no trial of its effect in this condition [r5].

medical.name: Corticosteroid injection (landmark- or ultrasound-guided)
medical.description: In an RCT of 180 patients with chronic bursitis, 40 mg methylprednisolone improved VAS and WOMAC pain and function more than PRP or shockwave at 1 and 8 weeks, although the corticosteroid group had higher baseline pain [r8]. In a 72-patient RCT all three injections (corticosteroid, oxygen-ozone, dextrose) improved symptoms, with corticosteroid effective at 1 week and ozone and prolotherapy better at 8 weeks [r9]. None had a placebo arm, and follow-up was 8 weeks or less. Response was seen even when ultrasound showed no bursitis [r3]. Infection of skin or soft tissue is the main contraindication [r18].

medical.name: Prolotherapy (20% dextrose) or oxygen-ozone injection
medical.description: In a single RCT of 72 patients, both were effective and their effect lasted longer than corticosteroid at 8 weeks. No placebo arm and short follow-up limit this finding [r9].

medical.name: Platelet-rich plasma injection
medical.description: In an RCT of 180 patients, PRP was less effective than corticosteroid at 1 and 8 weeks on pain and function, and better than shockwave on tenderness at 8 weeks. There was no placebo arm [r8].

medical.name: Surgery
medical.description: Reserved for patients who fail comprehensive conservative care [r5]. In 21 adolescents with a medial proximal tibial osteochondroma causing pes anserine syndrome, excision improved IKDC scores [r13]. No surgical series for pes anserine bursitis itself was identified.

medical.name: Injecting on a clinical diagnosis alone when the picture is atypical
medical.description: Clinical diagnosis had sensitivity 41.2% and specificity 59.5% against MRI, and the authors cautioned that clinical diagnoses may be inaccurate, particularly before invasive treatments such as injection [r6]. In another series only 2 clinically diagnosed patients (8.7%) had ultrasound evidence of tendinitis or bursitis [r3]. Consider imaging first when mechanical symptoms or osteoarthritis are present.

physio.name: Education and load modification
physio.description: Explain that the label is uncertain and that pain usually follows repetitive knee flexion and valgus load. Reduce or modify aggravating activity (stairs, hill running, cycling volume) to a tolerable level, rather than stopping all activity [r5].

physio.name: Address contributing factors (alignment, hip and knee control, load, weight)
physio.description: Assess valgus alignment, hip abductor and quadriceps control, foot posture and training load. Valgus deformity was associated with the diagnosis (OR 5.2) in a small study [r12], and a review recommends addressing biomechanical and systemic contributors [r5]. No trial tested these interventions.

physio.name: Stretching of the hamstrings, gracilis and sartorius
physio.description: Commonly prescribed, but no trial of stretching for this condition was identified. A single case report combined stretching with steroid injection [r15].

physio.name: Progressive loading of the knee flexors, hip and thigh muscles
physio.description: Extrapolated from tendinopathy loading principles. No trial in pes anserine pain was identified. Start with isometric holds and progress to heavier slow work as pain allows (clinical reasoning).

physio.name: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT)
physio.description: In a 60-patient open-label RCT of 3 weekly ESWT sessions against an ultrasound-guided injection, pain and pes anserine thickness fell in both groups, and quality of life improved more with ESWT [r10]. In a 180-patient RCT, ESWT was less effective than corticosteroid at 1 and 8 weeks [r8]. Neither trial had a placebo arm.

physio.name: Complete rest or prolonged immobilisation
physio.description: No source supports prolonged rest. The standard of care described in a review escalates from short-term rest to physical therapy [r5].

education: Pain over the inner side of the shin just below the knee is common, but the exact tissue source is uncertain, so the label is a working description.
Most people are managed without surgery. Reducing the aggravating activity, improving strength and control, and sometimes an injection are the usual steps.
An injection may reduce pain for weeks, but trials followed people for 8 weeks or less and did not use a placebo, so it is not a cure.
If your pain does not improve in about 8 weeks, or you develop locking, swelling, night pain or fever, tell your clinician so that the diagnosis can be rechecked.
Keep strengthening the leg and managing weight, since osteoarthritis and alignment often contribute.

rehab.overview: No rehabilitation trial for pes anserine pain was identified, so this program is built from clinical reasoning and tendinopathy loading principles. It is criteria-based, and it assumes that medial compartment osteoarthritis, meniscal, ligament, bone and nerve causes have been considered first [r5,r6]. Dosages are typical clinical ranges and not from a single source. As a working rule, pain during exercise should stay at or below about 3 to 4 out of 10 and settle within 24 hours (clinical convention). Review the diagnosis if there is no clear improvement by about 8 weeks, because response to treatment is commonly judged then [r5].

stages.name: Settle and modify load
goals: Reduce pain and irritability at the pes anserine insertion
Modify the aggravating load without stopping all activity
Maintain knee movement and quadriceps activation
Educate on the uncertain diagnosis and the plan
precautions: Stop or reduce hill running, deep flexion cycling and repeated stairs while irritable
Stay at or below about 3 to 4 out of 10 pain and settled within 24 hours (clinical convention)
Exclude red flags: night pain, fever, a hard mass or mechanical symptoms [r5,r13]

exercises.cues: Slide slowly through a comfortable range

exercises.name: Quadriceps set
exercises.cues: Press the knee down and tighten the thigh

exercises.name: Isometric hamstring hold (heel dig)
exercises.dosage: 5 × 20–30 s at about 50–70% effort, once or twice daily
exercises.cues: Press the heel into the floor with the knee bent to about 30°, with no sharp medial pain

exercises.name: Glute bridge
exercises.cues: Drive through the heels and keep the knees in line

exercises.name: Low-impact conditioning (pool or flat cycling)
exercises.dosage: 20–30 min, 3 times per week, below the pain threshold
exercises.cues: Keep the knee tracking over the second toe

progressionCriteria: Resting and walking pain at or below 2/10
Pain on stairs improving and settling within 24 hours
Isometric hamstring hold pain at or below 3/10
No night pain, effusion or mechanical symptoms

stages.name: Mobility and capacity
goals: Restore flexibility of the hamstrings, gracilis and sartorius if limited
Build isotonic strength of the hip abductors, hamstrings and quadriceps
Improve pelvic and knee control in single-leg stance
Return to normal walking and stairs without pain
precautions: Avoid sudden rises in running or cycling volume
Progress only when the previous session settled within 24 hours
Stop stretching into sharp medial tibial pain

exercises.name: Hamstring and medial thigh stretch
exercises.cues: Gentle, no sharp pain at the medial tibia. Evidence is limited to case reports [r15].

exercises.name: Single-leg glute bridge
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level and the knee in line

exercises.name: Side-lying clamshell
exercises.cues: Keep the feet together and the pelvis still

exercises.name: Standing hip abduction
exercises.cues: Upright trunk, with no lean

exercises.name: Step-up (low step)
exercises.cues: Control the knee over the second toe

exercises.name: Double-leg calf raise
exercises.cues: Pause at the top

progressionCriteria: Pain at or below 2/10 with daily activity and stairs
Single-leg stance and low step-up controlled with no dynamic valgus
Hamstring flexibility within about 10° of the other side (clinical convention)
No next-day increase in pain after sessions

stages.name: Strength and control
goals: Build heavier strength in the knee flexors, quadriceps and hip
Control the knee in single-leg tasks with no valgus collapse
Tolerate prolonged walking, stairs and cycling
Prepare for running and sport loading
precautions: Increase load in steps and check pain at 24 hours
Keep pain at or below about 3 to 4 out of 10 during sets
If there is no improvement by about 8 weeks, review the diagnosis and consider imaging [r5,r2]

exercises.cues: Torso upright, front knee over the second toe

exercises.name: Step-down
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level and avoid valgus

exercises.name: Romanian deadlift
exercises.cues: Hinge at the hips with a long spine

exercises.cues: Heels on a box, with a straight line from shoulder to knee

exercises.cues: Hip back, knee over the foot

exercises.name: Single-leg balance (unstable surface)
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level and the knee soft

Controlled step-down and single-leg squat with no valgus collapse
Hamstring and hip strength within about 10% of the other side (clinical convention)
No next-day flare after heavier sessions

stages.name: Return to running and sport
goals: Graded running, cycling or sport-specific loading
Change of direction and repeated knee flexion tolerance
Build a maintenance strength and load-monitoring routine
Return to full training with no symptom flare
precautions: Increase volume gradually (about 10% per week, clinical convention)
Avoid sudden hill or speed spikes
Stop and reassess if medial tibial pain rises or persists beyond 24 hours

exercises.name: Walk-to-run progression
exercises.dosage: Alternate 1–2 min running and 1–2 min walking, building to continuous running over 3–4 weeks
exercises.cues: Quiet, even footfalls with the knee tracking forward

exercises.name: Single-leg hop progressions
exercises.cues: Soft landing, stick for 2 s

exercises.name: Planned then reactive change-of-direction drills
exercises.dosage: 2–3 sessions per week, progressing speed and angle
exercises.cues: Lower the centre of mass, with the knee over the foot

exercises.name: Hill or stair running progression
exercises.dosage: Start at 25–50% of usual volume and build in steps (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Short strides and a soft knee

exercises.name: Heavy strength maintenance
exercises.cues: Keep the tempo controlled

progressionCriteria: Completes full training for at least 2 weeks with pain at or below 2/10
No next-day flare after the longest or fastest sessions
Strength and single-leg control about 90% of the other side (clinical convention)
Athlete confident, with a maintenance plan

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria for pes anserine pain were identified in the sources reviewed; the criteria below reflect clinical convention
Pain at or below 2/10 on stairs, single-leg squat and running, with no next-day flare
No tenderness at the pes anserine insertion beyond mild, and no effusion or mechanical symptoms
Hip, hamstring and quadriceps strength about 90% of the other side, and single-leg control with no dynamic valgus (clinical convention)
Tolerates graded running, cycling or sport volume for at least 2 weeks without a rise in pain
Other medial knee pathology has been excluded or treated, and a maintenance strength plan is in place
tests: Isometric hamstring, quadriceps and hip abductor strength with limb symmetry index
Pes anserine palpation tenderness (0–10) before and after loading
Weekly load and next-day pain log during the graded return

prognosis: The natural history of pes anserine pain was not identified in the sources reviewed, and no study followed patients beyond 8 weeks [r8,r9,r10]. Most people are managed conservatively, and surgery is rare, reserved for patients who fail comprehensive conservative care [r5]. After corticosteroid injection in osteoarthritis patients, pain and WOMAC scores improved significantly, but 8 of 17 reported no change in global assessment and the best responders were those with ultrasound bursitis [r3]. Because clinical diagnosis was inaccurate against MRI [r6] and the label overlaps with osteoarthritis and meniscal pathology [r2,r7], persistent pain should prompt review of the diagnosis. Anserine bursa pain was associated with falls over 2 years in an osteoarthritis cohort [r11].
prevention: Build running, cycling and stair volume gradually, and avoid sudden spikes (clinical reasoning; no prevention study was identified).

Maintain hip, hamstring and quadriceps strength and good knee control in single-leg tasks (clinical reasoning). Valgus deformity was associated with the diagnosis, but whether correcting control prevents it is unproven [r12].
Manage body weight and knee osteoarthritis, since they are listed as high-risk contexts [r5]. Trial evidence that this prevents pes anserine pain is lacking.
Address pain early with load modification, since the usual standard of care starts with rest and activity changes [r5].
Review falls risk in older adults with anserine bursa pain, because it was linked to incident falls [r11].
clinicalPearls: The label is contested: MRI showed bursitis in only 2.5% of 509 symptomatic knees, so do not promise the patient a bursa [r2].
Clinical diagnosis had sensitivity 41.2% and specificity 59.5% against MRI. Examine the joint line, MCL and medial compartment before attributing pain to the pes anserine insertion [r6].
Pes anserine pain commonly mimics a medial meniscal tear on presentation, so check the joint line and for mechanical symptoms [r2].
A response to injection does not confirm bursitis: in one series, improvement occurred in patients without ultrasound bursitis [r3]. Weigh this before escalating to repeated injections.
No exercise, stretching or manual therapy trial exists. Use pain-guided loading, address alignment and load, and review the diagnosis if there is no clear improvement by about 8 weeks [r5].
In an adolescent or young adult with persistent medial tibial pain and a palpable bump, image for an osteochondroma [r13]. If there is snapping and a normal MRI, consider dynamic ultrasound [r14].

forces.label: Valgus load on the medial knee

captions.text: A runner has recently increased his weekly distance and hill work.
Each stride loads the knee in flexion, with a tendency for the knee to drift inward (valgus).
The pes anserine tendons pull and glide over the medial tibia with every step.
Repeated load, not a single injury, irritates the medial proximal tibia.
Pain appears just below the inner side of the knee.
Zooming into the right knee from the front, on its medial side.

actions.text: Tender insertion: tendon, bursa or both?

captions.text: The pes anserinus is the conjoined insertion of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus on the medial tibia.
With repeated knee flexion and valgus load, the tendons pull and glide over the tibia.
The tendon area becomes thickened and tender. A bursa lies beneath the tendons.
Pain sits below the medial joint line, over the insertion.
But imaging often shows no bursal fluid, so the true source is uncertain.
The medial meniscus, MCL and medial compartment osteoarthritis can cause similar pain.
Diagnosis is clinical, and other medial knee problems must be excluded.
Schematic of a healthy bursa: a thin, lubricated sac that lets the tendons glide over the tibia.
Repeated friction irritates the bursa wall in this model of the condition.
The lining becomes inflamed and thickened.
Fluid can collect, but imaging finds this in only a minority of people with typical symptoms.
With load modification the irritation settles in this model. Real recovery times are not established.
